papers.title: FLMNet: Self-Ensemble Distillation from Masks to Seeds for Single-Tower CTR Prediction
papers.scoring_note: Separate mask disagreement from seed disagreement: regularize the former within a run and distill the latter across runs. The moment formulas require gates that do not read masked intermediate activations.
papers.summary: CTR self-distillation can be replaced with a computable disagreement penalty. FLMNet keeps gates on clean inputs and distills independently trained towers into one serving model. The distilled model reaches 0.8169 AUC on Criteo.

deep_reading.title: FLMNet: Self-Ensemble Distillation from Masks to Seeds for Single-Tower CTR Prediction
deep_reading.content:
CTR models such as FinalNet and QNN (a quadratic neural network) add a loss on top of the label loss that pulls the network toward its own averaged prediction. For example, the same network runs twice under two dropout masks, and both runs are trained toward their average. The trick works, but nobody has said clearly what it constrains. This paper, by authors at the National University of Singapore and USTC, gives the answer: ==as the number of masks goes to infinity, such an objective equals exactly "the label loss of the averaged score" plus a penalty on "the disagreement among the masked predictions"==. When the network structure meets three conditions, this penalty can be approximated in one deterministic forward pass, with no sampling. On that basis the authors design a single-tower model, FLMNet, and then distill towers trained from several random seeds into one student. On five public benchmarks the two FLMNet versions take the top two places in both AUC and Logloss. The absolute gains are small: on Criteo, AUC rises from the strongest baseline's 0.8156 to 0.8169. But the paper breaks down clearly where the gains come from.

## 1. The question: what does self-distillation actually constrain

FinalNet averages the logits of two interaction blocks and trains each block toward the average. QNN runs one network twice under independent dropout masks, freezes the average of the two predicted probabilities as a target, and pulls both runs toward it. In both, the "teacher" is an average over members of the model being trained, and no second model is needed at serving time; the authors call this family self-ensemble distillation.

Ablations in both original papers show that removing the term lowers AUC, but not by much. QNN drops only 0.06 percentage points on Criteo, and 0.17 and 0.19 on the smaller Frappe and KKBox; FinalNet drops 0.03 to 0.12. The two papers also explain it differently, one as knowledge shared between blocks and the other as mutual correction between runs that smooths the decision boundary, but neither has an experiment that isolates the mechanism.

There is another easy confusion. Members of a classical ensemble are independently trained networks from different initializations or data orders; members of a self-ensemble are just variants of one set of weights under different masks. The former sit in different "valleys" of prediction space, the latter all near one solution. The paper's approach is to treat these two disagreements separately: disagreement inside one tower is called mask noise, and disagreement between seeds is called seed noise.

![Two kinds of ensemble members (paper Figure 1). Left: members from one set of weights under different masks, close to each other, whose mean and variance can enter training directly; right: independently trained members, farther apart, whose pooled prediction serves as teacher. In both cases only one tower is served.](figs/2610.26143/intro_members.svg)

## 2. The objective under infinite masking: label loss plus a disagreement penalty

Let a sample's logit under mask $m$ be $z_m$, and the mean logit over all masks be $\mu$. Cross-entropy can be written $\varsigma(z)-yz$, where $\varsigma$ is softplus; the second term is linear in the logit and produces no extra term when averaged. So after taking the expectation over masks, the loss equals the cross-entropy of the mean logit, plus the term

$$A=\mathbb{E}_m[\varsigma(z_m)]-\varsigma(\mu)$$

This is the Jensen gap of softplus: the more the predictions agree, the smaller $A$. The paper proves that when the teacher is pooled in logit space, as the number of masks goes to infinity the self-ensemble objective converges to $\mathrm{CE}(y,\sigma(\mu))+\kappa A$, up to a term with zero gradient. Ordinary dropout training is exactly $\kappa=1$; QNN pooled in logit space has limit $\kappa=2$. ==In other words, what self-ensemble distillation adds beyond dropout is just raising the disagreement penalty's coefficient from 1 to 2==. Note that the original QNN averages probabilities rather than logits, and this exact result holds only for logit pooling.

$A$ is still an expectation over all masks and cannot be computed directly. The authors first bound it: $A$ is at most one eighth of the logit variance $V$, and the lower bound degenerates to 0 when the sigmoid saturates. The usual approach is a second-order Taylor truncation that keeps only the $V$ term, but on samples with large $V$ it underestimates $A$ several times over. The paper instead replaces the true mask distribution by a Gaussian of the same variance and evaluates the expectation with three-point Gauss–Hermite quadrature: the function is evaluated only at $\mu$ and $\mu\pm\sqrt{3V}$ and weighted 2/3, 1/6, 1/6, which approximates the expectation under the normal distribution. Compared row by row against a Monte Carlo value from 2,048 sampled masks on trained towers, the ratio of the Gaussian proxy to the true value always stays between 0.72 and 1.12, while the second-order truncation falls below a quarter of the true value on a few samples.

A practical conclusion follows. Keeping only the largest term of the expansion (the $V$ term above), $A$ is proportional to $V$, and $V$ is proportional to $\rho/(1-\rho)$ ($\rho$ is the masking rate), so $\kappa$ and $\rho$ act only through the "dose" $\kappa\rho/(1-\rho)$ and cannot be identified separately. An ablation that removes the distillation term without adjusting the masking rate changes only the dose, not the form of the objective.

## 3. A tower structure that makes the variance computable

The Gaussian proxy needs the mean logit $\mu$ and the variance $V$. The authors give three conditions under which both have closed forms: multiplicative gates read only unmasked inputs, the output layer is affine, and each layer only rescales its representation coordinatewise. Then the mean logit equals exactly the logit of the forward pass without dropout, and the variance also has an exact formula. The logit is a bias plus a weighted sum over hidden coordinates, and coordinate $j$'s value is the product of the factors each layer applies to it. Each layer's factor is $v_j(1+g_j+\eta_j)$: $v_j$ is this hidden coordinate's own mask factor, $g_j$ is the gate value without masking, and $\eta_j$ is the perturbation from masking the gate units, computed by multiplying each gate unit's output by its mask factor minus 1 and spreading the result over coordinates through the mixer. So one needs the expectation of the product of any two coordinates $j$ and $j'$. Since masks in different layers are independent, that expectation is a product over layers: each layer has a hidden-by-hidden table whose $(j,j')$ entry is $(1+\omega[j=j'])\,[(1+g_j)(1+g_{j'})+\omega K_{jj'}]$, and these entries are multiplied across layers. Here $\omega=\rho/(1-\rho)$ is the variance of a single mask factor and $g$ is the gate value; $K_{jj'}=\sum_k U_{jk}U_{j'k}r_k^2$ measures how many gate units the two coordinates share, where $r_k$ is the output of gate unit $k$ and $U$ is the linear layer mixing gate units into coordinates. The extra factor $1+\omega$ on the same coordinate comes from that coordinate's own mask; different coordinates are linked only through shared gate units. Weighting by the output weights $a_ja_{j'}$, summing, and subtracting the squared mean gives $V$.

QNN-α violates the first condition: its gate reads the masked output of the previous layer, so the random quantities of different layers become dependent. On Criteo, forcing the closed form onto trained QNN-α towers puts the mean more than three standard errors from the sampled mean on 76% to 81% of samples, and after training with the penalty the variance estimate is only 3.6% of the true value. This means training pushes down the estimate rather than the real disagreement. Simply letting the gate read the input embedding makes the formula exact, but lowers validation AUC by 10.5×10⁻⁴ without the penalty.

FLMNet's solution: each field's embedding feeds its own group of ReLU gate units, so no unit sees more than one field; a learnable linear mixing matrix then maps all units' outputs back to the tower's width, giving a gate value $g$ for each hidden coordinate, which is how one field's gate reaches every hidden coordinate. The representation is multiplied coordinatewise by $1+g$. Before entering the tower, the embedding is also recalibrated: in each embedding dimension, the fields' values in that dimension are summed with weights from a learnable field-by-field table, giving the field's adjustment for that dimension, and that coordinate is multiplied by "1 + gain × adjustment". The table compares three towers on the Criteo validation set (mean of three seeds, all with 4 layers and 5 gate units per hidden coordinate, which the paper calls 5 branches):

| Tower | Gate reads | Params | AUC (no penalty) | Closed-form penalty / Monte Carlo value (κ=2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| QNN-α | previous layer output | 3.05M | 0.81478 | 0.039 |
| QNN-α reading embedding | input embedding | 3.05M | 0.81373 | 0.998 |
| FLMNet | input embedding, per field | 3.14M | 0.81469 | 1.000 |

FLMNet is only 0.9×10⁻⁴ below the original QNN-α while keeping the formula exact. However, it changes three things at once, and this comparison only shows their combined effect.

![Where masks act in one tower layer (paper Figure 4, read bottom to top). Gates read the clean input embedding and masks fall only on the interaction path; this wiring decides whether the closed-form statistics hold.](figs/2610.26143/mask_flow.svg)

The exact variance needs, per layer, a table the size of the hidden dimension squared, two orders of magnitude more expensive than a forward pass, so it serves only as a ruler. The exact variance has two kinds of terms: those involving a single hidden coordinate, and cross terms linking two different coordinates. Training uses a truncated version: it keeps all of the first kind, and for the second it expands the product over layers as a polynomial in $\omega$ and keeps only the linear term, the part where only one layer's gate masks act at a time, dropping $\omega^2$ and higher. That costs just two extra matrix multiplications per layer. At the median over 24,576 validation samples, this truncation underestimates the variance by only 0.035%. For comparison, a coarser approximation that also expands the random masks on the gate units only to first order underestimates it by about 8%, which is why the authors use the first one. The appendix also records an engineering lesson. The authors once wrote the variance as the difference of two nearly equal large numbers, got negative variances, and wasted four training runs before finding the cause; they switched to a recursion in which every term is nonnegative.

## 4. Experiments: how much it gains, and from what

The five benchmarks are Criteo, Avazu, KKBox, Frappe and ML-1M, against seventeen models, all rerun by the authors under one protocol, mostly averaged over three to six seeds. Avazu's original validation and test sets have different positive rates (16.8% vs 15.2%), so the authors pooled them and re-split at random.

| Model | Criteo AUC | Avazu AUC | KKBox AUC | ML-1M AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DNN | 0.8136 | 0.7578 | 0.8502 | 0.9009 |
| FinalNet | 0.8151 | 0.7607 | 0.8515 | 0.9056 |
| QNN-α two heads | 0.8156 | 0.7568 | 0.8575 | 0.9052 |
| FLMNet-CF | 0.8162 | 0.7617 | 0.8581 | 0.9087 |
| FLMNet-KD | 0.8169 | 0.7620 | 0.8604 | 0.9099 |

CF is the single tower with only the closed-form penalty; KD is a student distilled on top of it from three CF towers. Measured by RelaImpr, the AUC gain over DNN (a plain multilayer-perceptron baseline) divided by DNN's margin above the 0.5 of a random ranker, the five-benchmark average is 1.36% for CF and 1.62% for KD, against 0.66% for the strongest baseline, two-head QNN-α. Before looking at the test set, the authors fixed for each benchmark an opponent (the strongest baseline on validation) and a lead threshold: comparing test AUC seed by seed, the mean difference must exceed twice its standard error (or a preset floor, whichever is larger). Below this is called the seed threshold. CF's lead is 1.9 to 8.7 times the threshold on every benchmark, but with only three to six seeds this is a lead under a pre-agreed rule, not a significance test.

The closed-form penalty is compared with three sampling-based regularizers, all on the same tower: dropout at $\rho=0.1$, the two-pass self-ensemble loss, and R-Drop (a regularizer that penalizes the difference between two dropout predictions). Across four benchmarks and three methods, 36 seed pairs in all, the closed-form penalty wins 34. Because dropout's dose is only a half to a third of CF's, the authors also raised dropout's masking rate to match the dose. On Criteo and KKBox the closed-form penalty still leads on every seed, by 6.5×10⁻⁴ and 23.9×10⁻⁴ on average. On Avazu its lead is only 1.9×10⁻⁴ and changes sign across seeds, suggesting the advantage there may come mainly from dose.

![Validation AUC difference between the closed-form penalty and sampling-based regularizers (paper Figure 7). In each group the first three solid stems are dropout, the self-ensemble loss and R-Drop, the dashed stem is dose-matched dropout, and open circles are single seeds; the vertical axis is a signed square-root scale in units of 10⁻⁴.](figs/2610.26143/fig7_dose.png)

Why does the penalty help? On Criteo with a fixed learning rate, the authors switch the penalty on or off mid-training. While it is on, the gap between validation and training cross-entropy grows by only about 0.3×10⁻³ per epoch, six to seven times slower than with no penalty; once it is off, the gap grows by more than 2.5×10⁻³ per epoch. So the penalty mainly slows overfitting. It also has a cost early in training: switching it on at epoch 4 gives a peak AUC 2.6×10⁻⁴ higher than switching it on from the start, and the run penalized from the start trails the unpenalized run from epoch 2 to 10. This experiment uses one dataset, a fixed learning rate and an onset tested every four epochs, so "epoch 4" should not be taken as a general setting.

![Timing of switching the penalty (paper Figure 8). Middle: taking the AUC gain of always-on over never-on as 100%, the share each schedule keeps; a slightly late onset is best, and the earlier it is switched off the more is lost; right: speed of overfitting, which depends only on whether the penalty is on.](figs/2610.26143/onset_sched.svg)

On the seed-noise side, by an identity, the amount by which a teacher pooling $K$ seeds beats the member average in Logloss equals exactly the Jensen gap between seeds, and it grows as $1-1/K$. The student retains about six tenths of it at every $K$. On Criteo, a student distilled from five seeds has AUC 0.80×10⁻³ above a directly trained member, and the teacher itself is 1.44×10⁻³ higher. The student does not start from scratch: it starts from one seed's fully trained model and is then distilled toward the teacher. As a control, continuing from that same starting point with labels only, no distillation, raises validation Logloss by 16×10⁻³, and in parameter space the direction the weights move under label training is nearly perpendicular to the direction they move under distillation, so the two change different parts of the model. The authors read this as the labels having no more generalizable information to give at this point; what remains is fitting to individual samples.

![Left: teacher gain against the number of seeds K, with orange points following the c(1−1/K) curve and blue squares the student gain; right: seed disagreement with the penalty divided by without it (paper Figure 10).](figs/2610.26143/fig10_seed.png)

The right panel shows the penalty barely reduces seed disagreement, with ratios between 0.80 and 1.30, and on Frappe it even grows. The two gains therefore largely add up. On Criteo and KKBox, where each single gain exceeds the seed threshold, using both retains 87% and 80% of their sum; on Avazu and Frappe the AUC differences among the four combinations are all within the threshold, so additivity cannot be judged.

On cost, on one V100, CF takes 46.7 ms per step, comparable to QNN-α's 45.4 ms with one head and 47.0 ms with two, because the saved second forward pass offsets the variance computation. But peak memory is about half again as high, 1,667 vs 1,106 MiB. KD needs $K+1$ training runs, and inference latency is about 5.8 ms for all.

## 5. Limitations

The authors list three boundaries. The closed form holds only for towers meeting the three conditions; training uses a Gaussian proxy, not the exact Jensen gap; and the gap between seeds has no closed form, so how much distillation recovers can only be measured. Also, the two gains are obtained separately, the penalty within one training run and distillation over $K+1$.

A few more points are worth noting. On the two advertising benchmarks all models are rerun at embedding dimension 10, and FinalNet and FinalMLP on Criteo come in 3.2×10⁻⁴ and 4.5×10⁻⁴ below their public leaderboard values, which the authors attribute to the leaderboard reporting a single tuned run. FLMNet uses a cosine learning-rate schedule and weight averaging; the baselines do not. KD students share some teachers and cannot be treated as independent repeats. All conclusions come from public offline benchmarks, with no online experiment.

## 6. Practical implications

If your ranking model already uses a two-pass dropout consistency loss, this paper gives two points you can check directly. First, see whether the teacher is pooled in logit or probability space, and whether gates read masked intermediate states; if the conditions are not met and you force the closed-form variance anyway, the model will "fool" the penalty. Second, when tuning such losses, tune the weight and masking rate together as one dose, and align dose before comparing regularizers, otherwise a difference in strength is easily mistaken for a difference in method.

Multi-seed distillation can be treated as a separate offline investment. It changes neither the structure nor the inference cost, but needs $K$ extra teachers; for frequently updated models, that training cost and freshness have to be counted together.

The student retains about six tenths of it at every K. On Criteo, a student distilled from five seeds has AUC 0.80×10⁻³ above a directly trained member, and the teacher itself is 1.44×10⁻³ higher. As a control, continuing from that same starting point with labels only, no distillation, raises validation Logloss by 16×10⁻³, and in parameter space the direction the weights move under label training is nearly perpendicular to the direction they move under distillation, so the two change different parts of the model. The authors read this as the labels having no more generalizable information to give at this point; what remains is fitting to individual samples.

The right panel shows the penalty barely reduces seed disagreement, with ratios between 0.80 and 1.30, and on Frappe it even grows. The two gains therefore largely add up. On Criteo and KKBox, where each single gain exceeds the seed threshold, using both retains 87% and 80% of their sum; on Avazu and Frappe the AUC differences among the four combinations are all within the threshold, so additivity cannot be judged.

On cost, on one V100, CF takes 46.7 ms per step, comparable to QNN-α's 45.4 ms with one head and 47.0 ms with two, because the saved second forward pass offsets the variance computation. But peak memory is about half again as high, 1,667 vs 1,106 MiB. KD needs $K+1$ training runs, and inference latency is about 5.8 ms for all.

5. Limitations

The authors list three boundaries. The closed form holds only for towers meeting the three conditions; training uses a Gaussian proxy, not the exact Jensen gap; and the gap between seeds has no closed form, so how much distillation recovers can only be measured. Also, the two gains are obtained separately, the penalty within one training run and distillation over $K+1$.

A few more points are worth noting. On the two advertising benchmarks all models are rerun at embedding dimension 10, and FinalNet and FinalMLP on Criteo come in 3.2×10⁻⁴ and 4.5×10⁻⁴ below their public leaderboard values, which the authors attribute to the leaderboard reporting a single tuned run. FLMNet uses a cosine learning-rate schedule and weight averaging; the baselines do not. KD students share some teachers and cannot be treated as independent repeats. All conclusions come from public offline benchmarks, with no online experiment.

6. Practical implications

If your ranking model already uses a two-pass dropout consistency loss, this paper gives two points you can check directly. First, see whether the teacher is pooled in logit or probability space, and whether gates read masked intermediate states; if the conditions are not met and you force the closed-form variance anyway, the model will "fool" the penalty. Second, when tuning such losses, tune the weight and masking rate together as one dose, and align dose before comparing regularizers, otherwise a difference in strength is easily mistaken for a difference in method.

Multi-seed distillation can be treated as a separate offline investment. It changes neither the structure nor the inference cost, but needs K extra teachers; for frequently updated models, that training cost and freshness have to be counted together.

papers.title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models
papers.authors: Jiang Wu, Yutong Song, Hongbo Wang, Guanghe Cao, Jeff Liang
papers.scoring_note: Train reusable content representations and personalized judgments jointly. Compression pays off in end-to-end serving only when repeated history prefill, input transmission, and scheduling are reduced too.
papers.summary: DuoLM precomputes one vector per item and uses a personalized ranker with user history and feedback. Shared history computation and a specialized runtime reduce online work. Throughput reaches about 26,400 candidate scores per second on one H100.
papers.key_insight: Train reusable content representations and personalized judgments jointly. Compression pays off in end-to-end serving only when repeated history prefill, input transmission, and scheduling are reduced too.

deep_reading.title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models
deep_reading.content:
DuoLM reads item content offline and reserves online computation for deciding whether a particular user will like it. An encoder language model compresses each item, while a ranker uses those representations with user history and feedback. The system design turns that reuse into measured serving gains.

## 1. Problem and motivation

A full-text cross-encoder reads item descriptions together with user context. Its representations depend on the request and cannot simply be cached across users. Repeating this work for every candidate makes language-model recommendation expensive.

A compact item vector is cheaper, but a generic text embedding may discard details needed for personalized judgments. DuoLM trains content compression and personalized ranking together.

There is also overhead outside the model. Candidates in one request share a user history, yet input construction, transmission, and scheduling can repeat. Prefix caching does not necessarily remove those operations. As model execution gets faster, they become a larger share of total cost.

![Training jointly learns the item encoder and ranker; serving precomputes item vectors and keeps personalized scoring online.](figs/2610.24481/framework-overview.svg)

## 2. Method

The encoder reads templated item text and uses its final EOS hidden state as one item representation. A continuous interface normalizes and calibrates its scale against the ranker’s native token embeddings. Both history items and candidates use this interface; textual feedback remains beside the relevant history entries.

During training, ranking gradients flow through the interface into the encoder. Item vectors are recomputed while learning and cached only after training. A frozen full-text teacher supplies scores for the exact histories and candidate groups used by the student. The student learns both observed targets and the teacher’s relative preferences.

The paper compares feedback in the encoder with feedback in the ranker. The former caches an item–rating pair; the latter caches one representation per item. Their quality is close, and the latter provides a simpler reuse boundary.

![Each candidate reads the shared history but cannot attend to another candidate, preserving independent scoring when candidates are batched.](figs/2610.24481/input-layout.svg)

At serving time, virtual token IDs reference a GPU-resident item-vector table. Requests carry IDs and feedback instead of transmitting complete vectors. These IDs are an access mechanism for continuous representations, rather than generated semantic item codes.

The multi-item scoring path prefills the user history once and shares its key–value cache across candidate branches. A tree-structured mask keeps branches independent. CUDA Graph replay further reduces launch and scheduling overhead. These changes save work at different points in the request path.

![The ranker reuses a shared history cache while each candidate follows its own scoring branch.](figs/2610.24481/scoring-example-single-column-compact.svg)

## 3. Main contribution

The central design boundary separates reusable content understanding from request-specific preference judgment. The representation is shared across users, the history computation is shared across candidates, and candidate scores remain independent.

The paper measures complete requests rather than treating lower model FLOPs as proof of faster serving. Runtime ablations help explain where the end-to-end improvement comes from.

## 4. Results

Recommendation quality is evaluated on Amazon Books and Video Games. NDCG@10 rewards relevant items appearing earlier in the ranking; absolute values should not be compared across datasets.

| Model | Books | Video Games |
|---|---:|---:|
| HLLM | 0.5508 | 0.5025 |
| DuoLM | 0.5586 | 0.5298 |
| Full-text teacher | 0.5440 | 0.5313 |

The student exceeds the teacher on Books and approaches it on Video Games. This demonstrates useful compression in these settings, not lossless compression for every domain.

On one H100, with 100 candidates per request, high-concurrency throughput reaches about 26,400 candidate scores per second. The unit is candidate scores, not user requests. Full-request p99 latency is about 537 ms at that concurrency.

The teacher comparison includes vLLM with automatic prefix caching. The gain combines a different model representation with a specialized serving path; it cannot all be attributed to switching inference engines.

Ablations also favor restraint: the simple EOS readout beats the tested learned readouts, stronger distillation does not keep improving quality, and extra hidden-state self-alignment hurts the reported setting.

## 5. Limitations

The evidence covers two product categories and specified hardware, without an online UGC search experiment. It does not establish behavior on rapidly edited posts, long comment threads, or breaking events.

Two engineering implications follow from the architecture. First, cached item vectors need versioning, incremental refresh, and memory budgeting. Moving encoding offline relocates its cost rather than eliminating it. Second, prefix reuse requires identical user history and context; candidate-isolation masks must remain correct.

Independent scoring also differs from list-level optimization for diversity or competition. Evaluation should preserve the paper’s candidate construction before expanding to a production recall pool. NDCG values from different candidate protocols are not interchangeable.

## 6. Practical implications

A content-rich ranking stage is a useful trial setting. Compare compressed and full-text scoring on long-tail items and narrow preference segments, where a single vector might hide important details.

Measure cache hits, history prefill, input preparation, and GPU execution separately. Report both candidate throughput and request throughput, plus tail latency. For UGC, include new and edited posts, recording the time until refreshed vectors become visible and the representation version used for ranking.

Sources: Sections 2–4 and Appendices A, C, and D. All figures are original assets from the paper’s arXiv HTML.

papers.title: When Semantics Fall Short: Persona-Guided Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Jundong Chen, Honglei Zhang, Shuai An, Enneng Yang, Han Yu
papers.scoring_note: Transfer user behavioral tendencies rather than relying on global item-text similarity. Local semantic links and persona-guided cross-domain links serve different purposes.
papers.summary: PerCDR uses inferred user personas to transfer behavior across domains, while local semantic relations strengthen within-domain modeling. On the Movie domain, NDCG@10 improves 15.40% over the strongest baseline.
papers.key_insight: Transfer user behavioral tendencies rather than relying on global item-text similarity. Local semantic links and persona-guided cross-domain links serve different purposes.

papers.title: Multimodal Decoupling for Diversified Recommendation through Semantic and Structural Shaping
papers.authors: Changran He, Jiaming Wei, Jianghong Ma, Tianjun Wei, Haijun Zhang, Xiaofeng Zhang
papers.scoring_note: Diversity depends on representation geometry as well as the final ranking objective. Compare accuracy-oriented and diversity-oriented configurations separately rather than combining their best numbers.
papers.summary: MOSS decouples multimodal features, alternates collaborative and semantic graph propagation, and regularizes category exposure. Its diversity-oriented configuration reaches 0.6348 Coverage@10 on Game.
papers.key_insight: Diversity depends on representation geometry as well as the final ranking objective. Compare accuracy-oriented and diversity-oriented configurations separately rather than combining their best numbers.

papers.title: Don't Rewrite the SID Map: Topology Preservation for Generative Retrieval in Dynamic E-Commerce Search
papers.authors: Jianbo Zhu, Xing Fang, Xiaopeng Chu, Mingmin Jin, Jing Wang, Bokang Wang, Jiaqi Ye, Xiang Zhang
papers.scoring_note: Treat code stability as part of the learned model. Small-beam hit rate and the fraction of remapped old items expose drift that a wide beam can conceal.
papers.summary: Updating semantic item codes can invalidate paths learned by a generative retriever. Preserving old codes, inserting new items, and warm-starting the model yields a 1.16% GMV lift in a three-week TmallAPP test.
papers.key_insight: Treat code stability as part of the learned model. Small-beam hit rate and the fraction of remapped old items expose drift that a wide beam can conceal.

papers.title: TaQFormer: A Treatment-as-Query Transformer with Data-Fusion for Multidimensional Treatment Modeling in Coupon Allocation
papers.authors: Jiahong Li, Zeqin Yang, Yu Xiang, Zhifan Jiang, Jingqi Ma, Enzheng Hua, Jixing Xu, Jun Wu, Fei Wang, Enyun Yu, Jiecheng Guo
papers.scoring_note: A frozen observational branch preserves broad patterns while a randomized-data branch corrects policy bias. Request-specific fusion makes their roles clearer than simply mixing the logs.
papers.summary: TaQFormer models interactions among category-specific coupon discounts. Observational pretraining is followed by randomized-data adaptation and request-specific fusion. At essentially unchanged subsidy cost rate, business value per user rises 1.26%.
papers.key_insight: A frozen observational branch preserves broad patterns while a randomized-data branch corrects policy bias. Request-specific fusion makes their roles clearer than simply mixing the logs.

papers.title: Structure-Aligned History Learning with Subspace-Structured Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Kaiwen Wei, Kejun He, Jie Zhang, Xiaomian Kang, Yuming Yang, Aijia Zhou, Xie Zhou, Yining Wang, Nayu Liu, Li Jin, Zhenyang Li, Jiang Zhong, He Bai, Jingxuan Wei, Junnan Zhu
papers.scoring_note: Align reconstruction units with the code hierarchy. Shuffle the preceding history while retaining current-item clues to test whether reconstruction truly uses the user trajectory.
papers.summary: SAHL reconstructs masked history at granularities defined by its structured item codes. This links item representation and persistent preference learning. NDCG@10 improves 18.6–30.0% over RPG across four Amazon categories.
papers.key_insight: Align reconstruction units with the code hierarchy. Shuffle the preceding history while retaining current-item clues to test whether reconstruction truly uses the user trajectory.

papers.title: OneChord: Distill What You Rank, Recommend in One Pass
papers.authors: Zesheng Li, Chengchang Pan, Honggang Qi
papers.scoring_note: Distill the distribution actually used for ranking, including its candidate set and normalization. Matching an intermediate code objective alone can leave a training–serving mismatch.
papers.summary: OneChord aligns recommendation supervision, refinement distillation, and serving through one normalized ranking fusion. Across six Amazon datasets, average relative NDCG@5 improves 7.12% over the strongest baseline.
papers.key_insight: Distill the distribution actually used for ranking, including its candidate set and normalization. Matching an intermediate code objective alone can leave a training–serving mismatch.

papers.title: SpecMRL: Redesign Matryoshka Representation Learning within Parametric Spectrum
papers.authors: Zhongxin Chen, Songhao Wu, Heng Cui, Cong Li, Xiao Zhou
papers.scoring_note: Compact embeddings need a useful coordinate ordering as well as useful information. Changing the readout basis can improve short vectors while retaining one shared representation model.
papers.summary: SpecMRL derives an ordered spectral basis from model parameters so compact embedding prefixes retain more useful information. On MTEB, half-dimensional representations exceed full-dimensional standard MRL.
papers.key_insight: Compact embeddings need a useful coordinate ordering as well as useful information. Changing the readout basis can improve short vectors while retaining one shared representation model.

papers.title: Candidate-dependent residual routing trades top-of-list accuracy for recall in sequential recommendation
papers.scoring_note: Recall gains can cancel a decline in first-hit rank. Inspect where additional hits appear before deciding whether a module belongs in candidate expansion or top-of-list ranking.
papers.summary: Candidate-dependent residual routing reweights a user history for each item. Paired-seed comparisons on REES46 show Recall@10 increasing 1.81%, with many new hits appearing lower in the top ten.
papers.key_insight: Recall gains can cancel a decline in first-hit rank. Inspect where additional hits appear before deciding whether a module belongs in candidate expansion or top-of-list ranking.
